### T-154 — The slow-step margin does not reach the registry's start steps

> _2026-09-26 · core/blong-gogo · open_

`log.slowMs` tunes the loader's steps and the retention store, and a runner may raise it for a
machine that is legitimately slow, but two callers of `withProgress` ignore it. `Registry.ts` passes
`getProgress` only for `create ports`, `start ports`, `ready ports` and `stop ports`, and
`core/blong-gogo/src/adapter/server/knex.ts`'s `ready` does the same for `schema table sync` and the
constraint pass, so all of them keep the compiled default of 1000ms and raising the margin cannot
silence them. If a slow startup ever warns under one of those labels, this is why. Give those calls
the configured margin — check first what the registry's `#config` carries, since the `log` block is
a platform-level sibling rather than part of the registry's section, while the knex adapter has the
same reach to `this.config`.

### T-183 — Log the gateway's effective port whether or not it was configured

> _2026-09-30 · core/blong-gogo · open_

Gateway.ts only speaks about the port when it was chosen at random, and only as a warn that is
suppressed at logLevel info and above: a statically configured port is never logged, and a random
one is silent in dev. Starting a gateway for the Storybook live modes therefore leaves an agent to
poll ss for a port it cannot be told about, and a server-only entry (gateway.port 0) gives no clue
either way. Emit the effective port once at startup — the configured value and the bound value — at
a level that survives the dev intent's log level.

### T-195 — Five helper modules still log a load error in their group folders

> _2026-10-04 · core/blong-gogo · open_

The loader gives every file in a handler group the shape of a handler and logs an error-level line
for a module that is not one. Five predate this: gatewayUuid.ts (blong-gateway adapter/db), core.ts
(blong-core adapter/db), oidc.ts, account.ts and accessModel.ts (blong-access adapter/db). Each run
prints Watch error loading X probably a generic source code was put in a handler group folder, which
is five error-level entries every suite run and trains a reader to ignore the stream that expected
errors were just cleaned up. Either the loader should skip a module that exports no handler and no
library, or those files should become libraries.

### T-225 — A watch reply arrives empty across the request boundary

> _2026-10-05 · core/blong-gogo · open_

The cluster adapter watch verb answers {events: asyncGenerator, existing} and what reaches the
controller carries neither key: a probe logged no existing and no stream, on a watch that opened
successfully and repeated once a second at the pacing floor.

Now explained: the whole reply is dropped, not the stream within it, and only on the path that
crosses a transport — the deploy port's request call. A handler reaches the same adapter through the
in-process proxy and receives both the initial list and the generator intact (see T-227 for the
probe). That is why a watch opened correctly and delivered nothing: the adapter was fine, and the
values were gone before the controller saw them. The realm therefore runs its watch from a handler,
and the resync interval is no longer the only trigger that works.

### T-228 — The k8s adapter's list answer carries no kind or apiVersion

> _2026-10-05 · core/blong-gogo · open_

A find answer here holds only metadata, spec and status on each item, while the API server returns
kind and apiVersion per item as well. Every caller therefore has to know the type from its own
request, which is what the kustomize diff had to be taught to do after it read eighteen objects as
obsolete beside eighteen creations (T-226).

Decide whether the adapter should keep the type identity the server sent, or whether a list is
documented as type-blind, and say so in the adapter so the next consumer does not rediscover it.
Worth checking first whether the loss is in the client library turning the response into objects
rather than in the adapter, since the same reply feeds the explorer and the deployment UI.

### T-250 — An unreachable database can kill a process by event

> _2026-10-06 · core/blong-gogo · open_

Found while fixing T-235 and not fixed with it. The knex adapter's start wraps ensureDatabase in
try/catch and warns, and the intent is plainly to continue: schema sync will surface the real
failure. What actually happened when the host did not resolve was a process-ending error with a
stack of one frame (getaddrinfo) and no await above it, which is the shape of an unhandled error
event on the mysql2 connection rather than a rejected promise the catch could see. Confirm it by
pointing a dev run at a name that does not resolve with the old code path, then make the failure
arrive through the caller: attach an error listener the moment the connection exists, or let
ensureDatabase reject in a way that does not also emit. It matters because a warn-and-continue that
kills the process is worse than a throw, which at least says where it came from.

### T-227 — The adapter replies null for a watch, and the generator dies there

> _2026-10-05 · core/blong-gogo · open_

Probed at the call site: cluster.custom.watch answers the packet
`[null, {mtid: response, method: cluster.custom.watch}]`, while cluster.custom.find answers real
data with the same coordinates, so the routing, the resource type and the group/version/plural are
all right and only the watch reply loses its value. The adapter carries no codec, so this is not a
wire encoding step, and it is not the meta wrapping either: what is left is the reply path around
the adapter handler.

Characterised on the second attempt. The loss is not in the adapter and not in the generator: a call
that reaches the adapter through a handler proxy carries the stream whole, and the realm's
kustomize.watch.run now logs "watch: open with 1 existing, stream present" and reconciles from the
list it receives. The call the port makes, through the deploy port's request path, is the one that
answers null. So the defect to fix is narrower than "a reply cannot carry a stream": a reply that
cannot be carried is replaced by a null instead of raising, and the caller cannot tell a dropped
result from an empty one. Fix the silence first (the reply path should refuse a value it cannot
carry), then decide whether the transport should carry the generator rather than only data.

### T-285 — The intents fixture ignores the config it is handed

> _2026-10-09 · core/blong-gogo · open_

Fixing the unused-variable lint error in frameworkRealms.test.ts meant renaming a parameter, not

case that builds a different config hands it to a mock that serves a fixed `{default: {}}` and
ignores the argument. The parameter was named `config` and unused, which is exactly what a reader

### T-316 — Debug mode should answer what the ACL guard would run for a call

> _2026-10-10 · core/blong-gogo · open_

`aclCheckSql` is pure and exported, but reaching it with a real configuration meant a throwaway
script that rebuilt the resolved ACL config by hand, printed the SQL and substituted the bindings
one by one; that script has been dropped with the rest of the investigation. The question it
answered — what does the guard actually run for _this_ call — belongs to debug mode, beside
`/api/sys/config`, `/api/sys/methods` and `/api/sys/rpc`: an `/api/sys/acl` that takes a method and
a record (or a table and an entity) and returns the resolved configuration (the guarded table, the
scope predicates, the path types), the SQL and bindings `aclCheckSql` builds for it, and whether the
action is guarded at all — an unknown `actionId` short-circuits the whole expression to `TRUE`,
which is itself the answer to a surprising number of "why was this allowed" questions. The party
investigation needed it because the entire per-request ACL cost is one 4 KB boolean expression with
four correlated `EXISTS` sub-queries, and reading that out of the source is not the same as reading
it for the call being debugged. It stays behind `systemDebug`, which must never be enabled in
production, and it should be read-only: it reports the SQL, it never runs it against a caller's
record.

### T-321 — The shutdown bound and the pod grace are the same 30 seconds

> _2026-10-11 · core/blong-gogo · open_

runServer.ts bounds the graceful stop at timeoutMs ?? 30_000 and no call site passes one, while
neither the operator tree nor the suite tree writes terminationGracePeriodSeconds — the 30 the pods
carry is the Kubernetes default. The two bound the same interval from opposite ends, so if
platform.stop() ever hangs, blong's force-exit and the kubelet's SIGKILL land at the same instant:
SIGKILL can win, the pod dies 137 part-way through teardown, and the graceful shutdown timed out
marker that would have explained it is lost. Kubernetes' own guidance is that the application must
finish before the grace period does, which leaves two remedies with different owners — the internal
bound sits below the default (25s is the usual number) or the generator writes an explicit
terminationGracePeriodSeconds with a margin for every process it deploys. The signal path itself is
verified and needs nothing: the operator and a suite service each print the marker and exit 0 in the
same second the signal arrives, and the spawn test in this package proves it for the CLI through GNU
timeout.

### T-340 — Enforce required and nested config keys once the schemas are complete

> _2026-10-14 · core/blong-gogo · open_

Config validation currently checks unknown top-level keys and type mismatches. Two checks are
deliberately deferred because the declared `validation` schemas predate enforcement and are
incomplete: `required` keys (testClient requires a `test` key its config never sets) and unknown
keys inside a declared nested object (`backend` gets `host`/`protocol`/`imports` from its realm,
none named in the schema). To finish: complete the schemas the repository ships (codec, adapter,
login, testClient, the framework realms), then enable the two checks in
`core/blong-gogo/src/configValidation.ts` - the schema is sealed only at the top level there, and
`required` errors are filtered in `validateConfigBlock`. Expect the same boot-failure sweep that
F-523 recorded; a suite that fails is a schema to complete, not a check to weaken.

### T-344 — A reload refuses a parent-declared key it would accept at startup

> _2026-10-14 · core/blong-gogo · open_

The allow-list a module is validated against is captured when it loads, so the parent-declared half
of it is the parent's block as it was at startup. An rc edit that adds a key to a parent's block for
a child is therefore refused by that child's reload validator — with `unknown key` — even though the
same key is accepted at startup, so a legitimate new setting needs a restart.

To close it, thread the parent's block getter down alongside `blockOf`: the child already receives
its own candidate block by `blockOf(snapshot)`, and the parent could pass `Object.keys` of the
candidate's block for this child, computed from the same snapshot, so the check judges a reload with
the keys the reload actually declares. The keysOnEntry set needs the same treatment, or a group
config added by an edit stays refused.

### T-350 — Stop keying a realm child by its function name

> _2026-10-15 · core/blong-gogo · open_

A minification setting should not decide which realms exist. The loader in
`core/blong-gogo/src/load.ts` looks a child's config block up by the child function's name and skips
the child when there is no such key, so any build that drops function names loses realms silently —
this session lost the whole `ui` realm of a built Storybook that way (F-537). Ways out, roughly in
order of how much they change: make the loader load a child whose name is empty anyway (its own
`config.default` block applies, which for blong-browser is the same activation), accept
`{name, load}` objects as children so the key is declared rather than inferred from a function name,
or at least log a warning naming the child that was skipped instead of a debug line. Whichever is
chosen, the app build's `minify: false` and the Storybook build's should no longer be load-bearing.

## Done

### T-341 — Validate a config reload and reject an invalid snapshot

> _2026-10-14 · core/blong-gogo · done_

The startup path validates every module's config block, but a hot reload is not validated:
ConfigRuntime.reload() builds the new snapshot, installs it and then notifies subscribers, so an rc
edit that introduces an unknown key is applied. The decision was to reject such a reload and keep
the previous snapshot. To finish: give ConfigRuntime a validator hook run before the snapshot is
installed, and collect one validator per module during the load. Each validator needs a getter that
re-derives its block from a candidate snapshot - capturing the parent's getter as a closure is the
natural way, which means threading the getter (or a path) through loadRealm's recursion; its call
sites are the loader's child calls and folderAnalysis' wrapper. Until then, document that only
startup is validated.

Done. ConfigRuntime gained setValidator, run before the installed snapshot: a rejected candidate
keeps the previous configuration, reports the rejection and yields an empty diff. The loader
collects one validator per module through a block getter threaded down the recursion, and the
watcher is attached at the end of the load because it did not exist where it was attached before.
Verified end to end with the watcher on. Design: D-548; the wiring defect found on the way: F-524.

### T-217 — Warn when a CLI config key matches no realm, port or framework key

> _2026-10-14 · core/blong-gogo · done_

A config override addressed one level too shallow is dropped in silence, which cost a long
investigation (@@F-370). The loader merges argv into the runtime config and then hands each port
only `mergedConfig[realm][port]`, so any key outside that slice is invisible: no validation error
and no log line. Emit a warning (or at least a debug log) when `--x.y=z` matches no realm, port or
framework key, so the next author sees the mistake in the first run instead of concluding that
config overrides do not work.

Implemented, more strongly than asked: a --x.y=z whose x matches no realm, port or framework key now
fails startup with the offending path named (@@D-547), and a key addressed one level too shallow
inside a realm or port is caught too (@@F-370). The one case deliberately left out of the check is
an rc-file key at the platform root, because a shared rc carries keys for every suite in the
repository.

### T-345 — The graceful-shutdown spawn test failed once in CI and passes locally

> _2026-10-14 · core/blong-gogo · done_

The graceful-shutdown spawn test in `core/blong-gogo/src/graceful-shutdown.spawn.test.ts` failed in
CI run 618 ("exit code 0 (graceful shutdown), got 1") but passes locally, with and without the
config allow-list rules, and inside the full 782-test suite. The likely cause is the run's timing on
a loaded runner: the test gives the spawned `blong` 10 seconds before SIGTERM and 5 more with
`--kill-after`, and the fixture's cold start is close to that (measured 9s here), so a slow runner
kills it instead of letting it shut down. Worth confirming with a longer timeout or by asserting the
marker without the exit code, and worth checking F-314 (a port held by an earlier aborted run)
before reading it as a code failure.

Resolved by the test itself: the fixture now asks for an OS-chosen gateway port, waits for the
readiness line before sending SIGTERM, forces an exit if the teardown hangs, and appends the child's
output to the failure message. Occupying 8080 reproduced the CI failure exactly (EADDRINUSE, exit 1,
no shutdown marker), so the timing suspicion in this entry was wrong; the full reasoning is in
@@F-528, and the test now runs in 0.8s instead of 10.
